title: Channel breakouts and choosing a lookback

inOneLine.simple: A channel marks the highest high and lowest low of the last few candles; a close beyond it is a breakout signal, and a shorter channel on the other side is the exit.
inOneLine.balanced: Most breaks fail and fall back inside, so the rule relies on the occasional break that becomes a long move. The lookback length changes the trades completely, and choosing it on past data is a common way to overfit.

explain.simple: The simplified version here uses the previous 20 daily candles for the entry [[channel]] and the previous 15 for the exit. A close above the 20-candle high enters long; a close below the 15-candle low exits. The channel leaves out the current candle, so a break means a close beyond every candle in the lookback. In Chart Lab, the Channel 20 overlay draws the 20-candle entry channel; count the 15-candle exit level from the candles. This is a simplified educational version, not any trader's system.
explain.balanced: A short lookback gives more signals and more [[false-breakout|false breakouts]]; a long one gives fewer, later signals. Comparing lookbacks is useful, but only if the final choice is tested on data that was not used to make it ([[out-of-sample]]). Gaps through the channel mean fills can be worse than the level, and the exit channel always gives back part of a gain before it triggers.

assumptions: Previous 20 candles: high 1.3150, low 1.2980; previous 15 candles' low 1.3060
Account 10,000 USD (simulated); 1 pip = 1 USD per 10,000 units
steps: Today closes at 1.3165, above 1.3150: a long signal.
The order fills at the next open, 1.3170. The stop at the 15-candle low, 1.3060, is 110 pips away.
1% risk = 100 USD. 100 ÷ 110 ≈ 0.91 USD per pip, about 9,090 units. Round down to 9,000 units.
Check: 9,000 units = 0.90 USD per pip; 0.90 × 110 = 99 USD at the stop.

assumptions: Illustrative practice test, not real results
Lookbacks of 10, 20, 40 and 60 candles compared on simulated years 1–3, then checked on year 4
steps: On years 1–3, the 40-candle lookback did best: +0.30R per trade.
Year 4 was not used to choose it. There, the 40-candle lookback gave +0.05R per trade.
The drop suggests part of the year 1–3 result came from fitting that data's noise.
Out-of-sample results are the fairer guide, and they are usually weaker than the best in-sample result.

explainSimpler: Draw a box around recent prices. Buy when price closes above the top, and get out if it falls below a smaller box.
commonMistake: Counting an intraday spike above the channel as a breakout. The simplified rules use closes only, so a candle whose high pierced the channel but closed inside it is not a signal.

quickCheck.prompt: The previous 20 candles' highest high is 0.6850. Which daily close triggers a long?

options.explanation: No: the high pierced the channel, but the close is inside it.
No: the close must be above the channel high, not equal to it.

quickCheck.prompt: A lookback chosen because it did best on years 1–3 does worse on year 4. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: It was partly fitted to the noise in years 1–3
options.explanation: Right: the best of many settings on one data set usually looks better than it is.

options.text: The year 4 data might be faulty
options.explanation: No: weaker out-of-sample results are normal, not a sign of bad data.

options.text: A shorter lookback is always better than a longer one
options.explanation: No: no lookback is always better; each trades differently.

doItNow.instructions: In Chart Lab, choose Breakout and turn on Channel 20. Mark each close beyond the channel. Then choose False breakout and count how many breaks fell back inside within 5 candles.

homework: Write down two lookbacks you would compare, and how you would keep some data aside to check the one you choose.
